title: Java Inheritance
learningObjectives: Explain inheritance as deriving a class from another class.
Use extends to declare a subclass.
Access inherited non-private members according to access rules.
Use super to refer to parent constructors or members.
Explain that Java classes have one direct superclass.

understand.concept: Inheritance lets a subclass extend a superclass and reuse or specialize its accessible members. The extends keyword establishes the relationship. Java classes have one direct superclass, although a class can implement multiple interfaces.
understand.whyItMatters: Inheritance can model a genuine is-a relationship and enable shared behaviour. It should be used when the subclass can safely satisfy the expectations of the parent type.
understand.analogy: Think of a well-designed object as a small service with a clear responsibility: it keeps the information it owns and exposes only the operations other code needs.
understand.analogyLimit: This analogy is only a design aid; Java access, inheritance and dispatch follow the language's exact rules.

explain.narrative:
## extends

Declare a subclass with `class Child extends Parent`. The child inherits accessible members and can add its own fields and methods.

## super

Use `super(...)` to invoke a parent constructor; it must be the first statement in a constructor. Use `super.method()` to call a parent implementation when appropriate.

## Inheritance limits

A Java class has one direct superclass. Private members are not directly accessible to subclasses. Prefer composition when a relationship is not truly an is-a relationship.

## Common mistakes

- Trying to extend more than one class.
- Forgetting the parent constructor call when no accessible no-argument constructor exists.
- Assuming private parent fields are directly accessible in the child.

questions.prompt: When is inheritance a good fit?
questions.answer: When the subclass represents a valid is-a specialization
